title: The 40,000-year-old flute
hook: Ice Age musicians carved a flute from a vulture's wing bone in a German cave.
peek: In 2008, archaeologists in a cave in southern Germany pieced together a slender flute made from a bird's wing bone. At around 35,000 to 40,000 years old, it is one of the oldest known musical instruments anywhere.
lede: Hohle Fels is a cave in the Swabian Jura hills of southern Germany. In 2008 a team led by the archaeologist Nicholas Conard found a dozen pieces of a hollow bone there. Fitted back together, they made a flute about 22 centimetres long with five finger holes. People were playing music in this valley at least 35,000 years ago, and probably closer to 40,000.

bullets.text: The flute is carved from the radius, a long thin wing bone, of a griffon vulture. These birds have wingspans of more than two metres, so their bones are long, straight and naturally hollow, a ready-made tube.
The maker cut five carefully spaced finger holes and two V-shaped notches at one end, probably where the player blew. Fine carving marks show the holes were placed by design, not worn in by accident.
Hohle Fels is not alone. Nearby caves such as Geissenklösterle have produced flutes of swan bone and mammoth ivory from the same era. In 2017 these caves became a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

Musicians have played copies of the flute and found it can produce a range of notes that sounds surprisingly familiar. Nobody knows what tunes Ice Age people played, but the instrument plainly was made to play more than one note.
